'''''Populus deltoides''''', the '''eastern cottonwood'''<ref name="PLANTS">{{PLANTS|id=PODE3|taxon=Populus deltoides|access-date=31 January 2016}}</ref> or '''necklace poplar''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a species of [[Populus sect. Aigeiros|cottonwood]] [[Populus|poplar]] native to North America, growing throughout the eastern, central, and southwestern United States as well as the southern Canadian prairies, the southernmost part of eastern Canada, and northeastern Mexico.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN|id=29382|name=Populus deltoides}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) - Flickr - Jay Sturner (1).jpg|thumb|left|A mature tree]]

''Populus deltoides'' is a large [[tree]] growing to {{cvt|20|-|30|m|ft|round=5}} tall and with a trunk up to {{cvt|2.8|m|ftin}} diameter, one of the largest North American [[hardwood]] trees. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is silvery-white, smooth or lightly fissured when young, becoming dark gray and deeply fissured on old trees.

[[File:Bark_on_bole_of_mature_Eastern_Cottonwood.jpg|thumb|[[Bark (botany)|Bark]] of a mature tree]]

The twigs are grayish-yellow and stout, with large triangular leaf scars. The winter buds are slender, pointed, {{cvt|1|-|2|cm|in|frac=4}} long, yellowish brown, and resinous. It is one of the fastest growing trees in North America. In Mississippi River bottoms, height growth of {{cvt|10|-|15|ft|m|0|order=flip}} per year for a few years has been seen. Sustained growth of {{convert|5|ft|m|sp=us|order=flip}} in height and {{convert|1|in|cm|sp=us|order=flip}} in diameter per year for 25 years is common.

The [[leaf|leaves]] are large, deltoid (triangular), {{cvt|4|-|10|cm|in|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|4|-|11|cm|in|frac=4}} broad with a truncated (flattened) base and a petiole {{cvt|3|-|12|cm|in|frac=4}} long. The leaf is very coarsely toothed, the teeth are curved and gland tipped, and the petiole is flat; they are dark green in the summer and turn yellow in the fall (but many cottonwoods in dry locations drop their leaves early from the combination of drought and leaf rust, making their fall color dull or absent). Due to the flat stem of the leaf, the leaf has the tendency to shake from even the slightest breeze. This is one of the identifying characteristics.<ref>Barnes and Wagner, Michigan Trees, University of Michigan Press, 2004</ref>

It is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with the [[flower]]s ([[catkin]]s) produced on single-sex trees in early spring. The male (pollen) catkins are reddish-purple and {{cvt|8|-|10|cm|in|frac=4}} long; the female catkins are green, {{cvt|7|-|13|cm|in|frac=4}} long at pollination, maturing {{cvt|15|-|20|cm|in|frac=4}} long with several {{convert|6|to|15|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=off|adj=on|sp=us}} seed capsules (samaras) in early summer, which split open to release the numerous small [[seeds]] attached to [[cotton]]-like strands. A single tree may release 40 million seeds a season.<ref name="usgs">USGS Aquatic and Wetland Vascular Plants of the Northern Great Plains: A successful, simple, reproducible, high frequency micropropagation protocol has been described by Yadav Rakesh et al., 2009 [https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs11816-009-0088-5] [https://www.npwrc.usgs.gov/resource/plants/vascplnt/species/popu.htm ''Populus deltoides''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071223063342/http://www.npwrc.usgs.gov/resource/plants/vascplnt/species/popu.htm|date=2007-12-23}}</ref><ref name=vplants>v-Plants (Chicago Herbarium): [http://www.vplants.org/plants/species/species.jsp?gid=32313 ''Populus deltoides''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070813162231/http://www.vplants.org/plants/species/species.jsp?gid=32313 |date=2007-08-13 }}</ref><ref name=silvics>{{Silvics |first=David F. |last=Van Haverbeke |volume=2 |genus=Populus |species=deltoides}}</ref>

== Variation ==
The species is divided into three [[subspecies]]<ref name=grin /><ref name=Eckenwal>{{cite journal|author=Eckenwalder, J.E. |year=1977 |title= North American cottonwoods (Populus, Salicaceae) of sections Abaso and Aigeiros |journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=193–208|doi=10.5962/bhl.part.29239 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or up to five [[Variety (botany)|varieties]].<ref name=plantlist>{{citation|title= The Plant List: A working list of all plant species |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and Missouri Botanical Garden |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl/record/tro-50295598}}</ref> The subspecies classification is as follows:
*'''''Populus deltoides'' subsp. ''deltoides''''',  '''eastern cottonwood''' is found in southeastern Canada (the south of [[Ontario]] and [[Quebec]]) and the eastern United States (throughout, west to [[North Dakota]] to [[Texas]]).
*'''''P. d. monilifera''''' (Aiton) Eckenw., the '''plains cottonwood''' (syn. ''P. deltoides'' var. ''occidentalis'' Rydb.; ''P. sargentii'' Dode) ranges from southcentral Canada (southern [[Alberta]], [[Saskatchewan]], and [[Manitoba]]) to the central United States and south to northern [[New Mexico]] and [[Texas]]. It is the state tree of [[Wyoming]].
*'''''P. d. wislizeni''''' (S.Watson) Eckenw., the '''Rio Grande cottonwood''' (syn. ''P. wislizeni'' (S.Watson) Sarg.; ''P. fremontii'' var. ''wislizeni'' S.Watson) grows from southern [[Colorado]] south through [[Texas]] to northeastern Mexico ([[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[San Luis Potosi]]), and west to [[Arizona]]. GRIN records its presence in [[California]];<ref name=grin /> the Jepson ''Flora of California'' does not.<ref name=jeps>Jepson Flora: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Populus ''Populus'']; clicking 'next taxon' through the genus shows no entry for this taxon</ref> Some sources identify this subspecies by the epithet "''wislizenii''"; per ICN article 60C.2, the spelling is with one "i".<ref>J. McMeill et al. (eds). 2012. International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants. Regnum Vegetabile 154. Koeltz Scientific Books. {{ISBN|978-3-87429-425-6}}</ref>

== Range ==
The range of the eastern cottonwood is very large, stretching from southwestern Mexico northwards to the southern provinces of Canada and from New Hampshire to Oregon.<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=30102841-2 |title=''Populus deltoides'' W.Bartram ex Marshall |access-date=15 January 2026}}</ref> In Mexico, it is mainly present as subspecies ''wislizeni'' and it is native only to the state of [[Jalisco]] in the southwest. In the northwest, it only grows in the state of [[Sonora]]. In contrast, it is found in about half the states of northeastern Mexico including [[Aguascalientes]], [[Coahuila]], [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Durango]], [[Nuevo León]], and [[Zacatecas]]. It is also present in the Gulf Coast state of [[Veracruz]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |date=21 December 2025 |title=''Populus deltoides'' in Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 25.12 |url= http://www.worldplants.de?name=Populus-deltoides |website=World Plants |language=en |access-date=15 January 2026}}</ref>

In the southwestern United States, the species is native as far west as a few locations in Utah and Arizona according to the USDA [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] (NRCS) and is fairly widespread in both New Mexico and Texas.<ref name="NRCS">{{PLANTS |date=2026 |symbol=PODE3 |taxon=Populus deltoides |access-date=15 January 2026}}</ref> In the Pacific Northwest, [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO) reports it as native to Washington, Oregon, and Idaho,<ref name="POWO" /> however the NRCS only reports as far west as Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado.<ref name="NRCS" /> To the east, it is native to every state of the central and southeastern United States, including Florida along northern parts of the Gulf Coast.<ref name="NRCS" /> The NRCS also reports in every state of the northeast,<ref name="NRCS" /> but POWO does not list it in Maine or Rhode Island.<ref name="POWO" />

In Canada, eastern cottonwoods grow in the most southerly edge of Quebec and southern areas of Ontario, mainly near Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. To the west, they are widespread into southern Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Little |first1=Elbert L. Jr. |author-link1=Elbert Luther Little |date=1971 |title=Atlas of United States Trees |url=https://archive.org/details/CAT87209954 |url-access=registration |language=en-us |volume=1. Conifers and Important Hardwoods |location=Washington, D.C. |publisher=US Department of Agriculture, Forest Service |pages=Map 149–W, Map 149–E |access-date=15 January 2026}}</ref> It is also reported as native to British Columbia by both the NRCS and POWO.<ref name="NRCS" /><ref name="POWO" />

== Ecology ==
Eastern cottonwood needs bare soil and full sun for successful germination and establishment; in natural conditions, it usually grows near [[river]]s, with mud banks left after [[flood]]s providing ideal conditions for seedling germination; human soil cultivation has allowed it to increase its range away from such habitats.<ref name=silvics />

Clonal reproduction producing stands does occur in ''Populus deltoides'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.threeriversparks.org/blog/species-spotlight-eastern-cottonwood|title=Species Spotlight: Eastern Cottonwood|website=Three Rivers Park District|location=Plymouth, Minnesota|last=Kortebein|first=Paul|date=27 July 2020|access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref> though to a more limited degree than in related species such as ''[[Populus tremuloides]]'' or quaking aspen, and it will resprout readily when cut down.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bhort.bh.cornell.edu/tree/cottonwood.htm|title=16. EASTERN COTTONWOOD|website=Know Your Trees|publisher=L.H. Bailey Hortorium|date=22 May 2002|last1=Cope|first1=J.A.|last2=Winch|first2=F.E. Jr.|last3=Cope|first3=E.A.|access-date=8 August 2026|location=Ithaca, New York}}</ref>

The leaves serve as food for [[caterpillar]]s of various [[Lepidoptera]], including [[poplar tentmaker]]s, [[Oedemasia concinna|redhumped caterpillar]]s and [[fall webworm]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uky.edu/Ag/Entomology/treepestguide/cottonwd.html|title=Cottonwood (''Populus deltoides'')|website=Guide to Insect Pests of Woody Plants|publisher=University of Kentucky College of Agriculture|location=Lexington, Kentucky|last1=Townsend|first1=L.|last2=Larson|first2=J.|date=20 February 2020|access-date=8 August 2026|others=Website design by P. Dillon}}</ref>

== Uses ==
The wood of eastern cottonwood is typical of the ''Populus'' family in its softness, weighing just {{convert|28|lb/cuft|abbr=in|order=flip}}. It is utilized for things like plywood and interior parts of furniture.

[[General Custer]] fed his horses and mules the bark during the 1868–69 winter campaign against Native American tribes south of Arkansas. According to [[Charles Goodnight]], cowboys afflicted with gastric disorders would make an astringent tea from the inner bark.<ref>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |pages=335–36}}</ref>

== Oldest and largest ==
[[File:Cottonwood 20090521 083459 1.jpg|thumbnail|Seeds and seed hairs from an eastern cottonwood]]
Eastern cottonwoods typically live 70–100 years, but they have the potential to live 200–400 years in ideal conditions.

The [[Balmville Tree]] (felled in 2015 at approximately 316 years old) was the oldest eastern cottonwood in the United States.<ref name="Tree cutdown story">{{cite news|last=Sparks|first=Leonard|title=Sad farewell to Balmville Tree|url=http://www.recordonline.com/article/20150805/NEWS/150809658|newspaper=[[Times-Herald Record]]|date=August 6, 2015|access-date=August 5, 2015}}</ref>

*The US national champion ''Populus deltoides'' var. ''deltoides'' is located in [[Beatrice, Nebraska]] and measures {{cvt|88|ft|m|order=flip}} tall, {{cvt|108|ft|m|order=flip}} wide.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/eastern-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-deltoides-3/ |title=Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides ssp. deltoides) |author=American Forests |year=2013 |access-date=July 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160816173610/http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/eastern-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-deltoides-3/ |archive-date=August 16, 2016 }}</ref>
*The US national champion ''Populus deltoides'' var. ''monilifera'' is located in [[Ravalli County, Montana]] and measures {{cvt|112|ft|m|order=flip}} tall, {{cvt|94|ft|m|order=flip}} wide.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/plains-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-monilifera-3/ |title=Plains Cottonwood (''Populus deltoides'' ssp. ''monilifera'') |author=American Forests |year=2012 |access-date=July 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223100237/http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/plains-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-monilifera-3/ |archive-date=February 23, 2016 }}</ref>
*The US national champion ''Populus deltoides'' var. ''wislizeni'' is located in [[Bernalillo County, New Mexico]] and measures {{cvt|84|ft|m|order=flip}} tall, {{cvt|83|ft|m|order=flip}} wide.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/rio-grande-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-wislizeni-3/ |title=Rio grande Cottonwood (''Populus deltoides'' ssp. ''wislizeni'') |author=American Forests |year=2012 |access-date=July 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223111243/http://www.americanforests.org/bigtree/rio-grande-cottonwood-populus-deltoides-ssp-wislizeni-3/ |archive-date=February 23, 2016 }}</ref>

The largest recorded cottonwood tree in the world is the Frimley Park tree located in Hastings, New Zealand and measures {{cvt|138|ft|m|order=flip}} tall, {{cvt|111|ft|m|order=flip}} wide and {{cvt|33.4|ft|m|order=flip}} in girth.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://register.notabletrees.org.nz/tree/view/210 | work = The Zealand Tree Register | title = Tree Information | access-date = 18 April 2018}}</ref> This cottonwood was planted in the 1870s.

== Symbolism ==
Calling the cottonwood tree "the pioneer of the prairie", the Kansas state legislature designated the cottonwood the official state tree of [[Kansas]] in 1937.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Q_lOAAAAIBAJ&pg=5320%2C4181963 | title=Tidbits | work=Ludington Daily News | date=Aug 4, 2001 | access-date=15 October 2015 | page=33}}</ref> It became the state tree of [[Wyoming]] in 1947,<ref>{{citation  |title= Wyoming facts and symbols |publisher= State of Wyoming |url= http://www.wyo.gov/about-wyoming/wyoming-facts-and-symbols |access-date= 6 December 2019}}</ref> and that of [[List of Nebraska state symbols|Nebraska]] since 1972.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nebraska Secretary of State |date=3 October 2019 |url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/symbols/tree.html |access-date=5 November 2019}}</ref>
